# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–19 (Complete – Updated 140)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fifth year** (Chapter 19). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; Pitt and Lady Jane visit Queen's Crawley. Sir Pitt collapses after heavy drinking, dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Within three-to-four days of inheriting, Pitt determines to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies (described with autumn details: frost silvering hedges, baker's boy late, line at oven long, light going early, cart with turnips, rain threatening after thaw). Body of late Sir Pitt lies in his apartment, watched unceasingly by professional attendants (woman or two, three or four undertaker's men from Southampton, dressed in black, playing cards and drinking beer in housekeeper's room when off duty).
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City, Piccadilly, Bowls's lodging-house), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calaus, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender, May Fair, Chapel in May Fair, Cape Town, Finchley Common, Mirecombe.

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED (Summer 1816)**
- Nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago. **Final days and death (Chapter 18)**: Collapsed after heavy rum-and-water drinking; became "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." Died summer 1816; all blinds pulled down; church bell tolled; chancel hung in black. **Chapter 19 funeral**: Body placed in his apartment at Queen's Crawley; watched unceasingly by professional attendants; housekeeper's room serves as their rendezvous; watchers and lights perpetually burning in closed room; coffin placed at end of passage; elaborate funeral ceremony in autumn with many townspeople assembled in black.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Now Baronet, MP (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon father's death**: Immediately plans to clear estate with ready money. Within three-to-four days, bearing changed; fixes plans to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be friendliest terms with blood relations. Called Lady Southdown "Lady Macbeth"; when she waited for weakness, rose scared and left library. Told her she won't go away; she let house at Brighton, spent dividends. **Chapter 19 funeral occasion**: In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Heightened colour; shook Rawdon by hand; saluted Rebecca with handshake and low bow. Has gotten fat; doing the thing handsomely (per Rawdon's assessment). **Toward Rebecca (Chapter 19)**: Remembered her testimonies of respect and veneration from early days; disposed favorably. Acknowledged marriage improved Rawdon (clear from altered habits and demeanor); owned he owed his fortune to it; smiled inwardly as cunning diplomatist recognizing lucky union. Reports from Lady Jane increased his favorable impression. **Third day after funeral, at dinner**: Actually said to Rebecca, "Ahem! Rebecca, may I give you a wing?"—speech that made her eyes sparkle with pleasure.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon Pitt's letter (Chapter 18)**: But half-pleased; thought "What's use of going down to stupid place?" **Wife's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Rebecca tells him she means for him to get Parliament seat, for herself Court presentation, for him place through Lord Steyne's influence. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: Turned red passing through old hall with Rebecca, arm in arm. Abashed; recollections of boyhood, innocence, Eton, mother, dead sister he was passionately fond of, how he used to thrash Pitt. Encouraged by Lady Jane's affection, twirled mustachios and saluted her with kiss, causing her to blush exceedingly. Called her "dev'lish nice little woman." Agreed with Rebecca that Pitt got fat and doing thing handsomely; "he can afford it." **Upon return to May Fair**: Exploded with loud laughter when Rebecca described her victimization by Lady Southdown's medicine; enjoyed the entertainment with Lord Steyne and son in London. Reported as improved by marriage in habits and demeanor.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Character and social position (Chapter 18)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; displays herself at gatherings; sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. Manipulates husband through derision. **Chapter 19 social maneuvering (Funeral period)**: Somewhat pale passing through old hall; pinched husband's arm entering oak parlour. **With Lady Jane**: Lady Jane's embrace brought tears to eyes of "little adventuress"—which ornaments she wore very seldom. Artless mark of kindness and confidence touched and pleased her. Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Lady Jane informed Sir Pitt she thought Rebecca kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With sisters-in-law**: Did not attempt to forget former position of Governess; recalled it frankly and kindly; asked about studies with great gravity; told them she thought of them many days and longed to know of welfare; made it appear she had not ceased keeping them uppermost in thoughts and taking tenderest interest since leaving them. **With Lady Southdown (Chapter 19)**: Attacked her on nursery question; claimed her own little boy was saved by calomel freely administered when Paris physicians gave up; mentioned hearing of her from Reverend Lawrence Grills, Minister of chapel in May Fair which she frequented; described how views changed by circumstances and misfortunes; hoped past worldliness and error might not incapacitate her from serious thought; described indebtedness to Mr. Crawley for religious instruction; touched upon Washerwoman of Finchley Common, read with greatest profit; asked about Lady Emily (author), now Lady Emily Hornblower at Cape Town where husband hopes to become Bishop of Caffraria. **After funeral**: Felt very agitated and unwell; requested Lady Southdown's medical advice. Lady Southdown came privately at night in bed-gown, looking more like Lady Macbeth than ever, with parcel of favorite tracts and medicine of her own composition, which she insisted Rebecca take. Rebecca accepted tracts, examined with great interest, engaged Dowager in conversation about them and welfare of soul to escape medication. But after religious topics exhausted, Lady Macbeth would not quit Rebecca's chamber until cup of night-drink was emptied; Rebecca compelled to assume look of gratitude and swallow medicine under Dowager's unyielding nose. **Upon return to May Fair**: Countenance very queer when Rawdon heard what happened; described occurrence to him with fun she could not disguise despite expense to herself. Acted whole scene for Lord Steyne and son: put on night-cap and gown, preached great sermon in serious manner, lectured on virtue of medicine with perfect imitation of Countess's Roman nose. "Give us Lady Southdown and the black dose" became constant cry in her little drawing-room in May Fair. **First time**: Dowager Countess of Southdown was made amusing. **Eyes sparkle**: When Sir Pitt offered her a wing at dinner on third day after funeral.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **London period (Chapter 18)**: Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen, scarcely noticed by mother; passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. **Relationship with father unchanged**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews mornings during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books; walls covered with pictures. Takes accustomed morning walks with father and pony. **Chapter 18 plan**: Rebecca forbids him traveling to Queen's Crawley; let him stay in nursery.

**Miss Briggs (Chapter 19)**
- **Background**: Miss Crawley's faithful retainer for score of years; received little annuity from Miss Crawley's legacy. **Dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Lady Southdown dismissed her as quickly as decency permitted; Mr. Pitt made no objection. **Post-dismissal and reunion (Chapter 19)**: Fatigued from weary walk to Times Office in City inserting advertisement for sixth time; reached Mr. Bowls's door where she lodged. Rebecca recognizes her, pulls up carriage, embraces warmly. They retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour; Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Briggs told all her history amidst sobs and wonder; Rebecca gave narrative with artlessness and candour. **Mrs. Bowls's warning**: Cautioned Briggs against venturing into "lion's den." Briggs promised to be cautious. **Outcome**: Briggs went to live with Mrs. Rawdon next week; within six months lent Rawdon Crawley six hundred pounds upon annuity.

**Lady Jane Crawley (now Lady Pitt) (Chapter 19)**
- **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Takes both hands of sister-in-law and kisses her affectionately. Embrace brought tears to Rebecca's eyes. Blushes exceedingly when Rawdon salutes her with kiss. Called "dev'lish nice little woman" by Rawdon. **With Rebecca**: Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Engaged in confidential medical conversation about children and ailments (typical of mothers and women). Informed Sir Pitt she thought her new sister-in-law kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With mother**: Busy with her nursery as far as mother would let her; sighs wishing mother would not insist on giving so much medicine; often thinks they should all be better without it.

**Lady Southdown (Dowager Countess) (Chapter 19)**
- **Funeral occasion**: Preserves solemn stony silence in company of Pitt and rebellious wife; frightens children in nursery with ghastly gloom. Only faint head-dress bending welcomed Rawdon and Rebecca. **With Rebecca**: Comes privately at night in bed-gown looking more like Lady Macbeth than ever; brings parcel of favorite tracts and medicine of her own composition; insists Rebecca take it; will not quit chamber until cup of night-drink is emptied. Later becomes subject of mockery and entertainment in Rebecca's drawing-room in May Fair; made amusing for first time in her life through Rebecca's imitations.

**Rosalind and Violet (Pitt's sisters) (Chapter 19)**
- Young women summoned from school for funeral. **Rosalind**: Replies with great liberality that person can't help their birth; agrees with brother Pitt that as Rebecca is in family, they are bound to notice her; notes Aunt Bute wants to marry Kate to young Hooper, wine-merchant, and asked him to Rectory for orders. **Violet**: Refuses to read Washerwoman of Finchley Common; avoids passage at end of which coffin placed with watchers and lights; comes down to family dinner.

**Other Characters Status**: Bowls and Firkin (received legacies, married, set up lodging-house); Mrs. Bowls cautious of Rebecca; Colonel Dobbin, Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Lord Steyne, Reverend Bute Crawley, James Crawley, Miss Horrocks (married to saddler at Mudbury), Hester (maid), Horrocks (butler) unchanged; Reverend Lawrence Grills (Minister of chapel in May Fair); Lady Emily Hornblower (née author of Washerwoman of Finchley Common, now at Cape Town); Conar (complains of aching back as usual).

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt dies summer 1816**: Collapses after heavy drinking; becomes helpless; dies after days of decline; body watched by professional attendants at Queen's Crawley.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt, Baronet and MP**: Within days determines to rule justly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations.
- **Briggs dismissed but connected**: Released by Lady Southdown; reconnects with Rebecca who invites her to live with them; lends Rawdon six hundred pounds within six months.
- **Funeral at Queen's Crawley (Autumn 1816)**: Rawdon and Rebecca return; Pitt has gotten fat; Lady Jane warmly greets Rebecca, bringing tears; Lady Southdown maintains cold silence; sisters present; elaborate mourning ceremony; body watched by undertaker's men.
- **Rebecca's strategic maneuvering (Chapter 19)**: Wins Lady Jane's affection within half hour (becomes intimate friends); skillfully manipulates Lady Southdown through flattery, religious conversation, medicine acceptance, and feigned deference, though becomes subject of mockery and imitation upon return to May Fair; wins Sir Pitt's favor through remembered respect from early days and reports from Lady Jane; receives compliment from Sir Pitt on third day after funeral (wing offer).
- **Rebecca's nature**: Manipulates through charm and calculated deference; capable of genuine tears; enjoyed social recognition; performs and entertains for social advancement; witty mimic; still controls Briggs through financial dependence despite lending six hundred pounds; maintains facade of kindness toward sisters while advancing socially.
